opus-5.5.text:
I'd describe it as very exploratory, almost deliberately unstructured. That summer, nobody was handing out a fixed roadmap saying "here's the product, go build feature X." The attitude was more like: code is a really interesting domain for machine learning, because it's structured, it's verifiable, and there's a huge amount of it, so let's find out what's actually possible.

A lot of the work came from people trying different ideas in parallel. Someone would look at program synthesis, someone else at learning from code repositories or code review, and someone else at how models could help developers in their day-to-day workflow. Small experiments came first. If something showed promise, the group would lean in. If it didn't, people moved on fairly quickly without much attachment.

As an intern, I found that culture really freeing. You were encouraged to ask "what if" questions and to prototype quickly, even if the idea sounded a bit far-fetched at the time. Looking back, a lot of what people were poking at then, like models that understand and generate code, turned out to point in the direction the whole field later went. Back then it felt more like curiosity-driven research than a clear bet, but that openness was exactly what made it a great place to learn.

r001.rationale: The response describes parallel experiments and quick prototypes, says promising ideas received more attention, and notes that interns were encouraged to explore ideas—communicating experimentation as a way to find promising directions that summer.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the word I'd use is "unstructured" in the best sense. When I joined the Google X team that summer, I expected the usual research-internship setup where you're handed a well-scoped problem and you spend three months chipping at it. It wasn't like that at all. The group was small, and the whole mandate was basically "we think large models can change how people write code, go figure out where that's actually true."

So a lot of the early weeks were just trying things. Someone would have a hunch, maybe about code completion inside a specific editor, or about using the model to explain a diff, or about generating test cases, and we'd build a scrappy prototype in a few days and put it in front of real engineers. The bar for killing an idea was low. If people didn't naturally reach for the tool again after the first day, that told us something, and we'd move on without much ceremony.

What I appreciated was that it was very bottom-up. Nobody was dictating the roadmap. The leads treated interns and full-time researchers roughly the same, which meant if I had a direction I believed in, I could just go pursue it and the burden was on me to show evidence. That was a bit uncomfortable at first, because there's no one telling you whether you're on the right track. But it taught me to think about what the signal of success looks like before building anything.

The other thing I'd say is that they cared about the user side almost more than the modeling side. The question was never just "can the model do this," it was "will an engineer at Google actually want this in their workflow." That framing stuck with me, and a lot of how I think about systems work today, including the stuff I did later on serving infrastructure, traces back to that summer of watching ideas live or die based on whether people kept using them.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes interns pursuing their own ideas, quickly prototyping them, and using engineers’ responses to decide which directions to continue or abandon.
